fossil_curator.text: Have a look at these fish. Fossils, about 385 million years old, from the bed of Lake Orcadie, a vast lake that covered Caithness and Orkney when the fish were only just getting the hang of having jaws.
Caithness flagstones are full of them. Splitters in the quarries would open a slab like a book and find a fish lying in it, perfect, like it had swum in yesterday.
The gallery upstairs is the Swanson, named for the family whose gift built it. Art downstairs, books upstairs, fish everywhere.

robert_dick_fan.text: Robert Dick was a baker who found the northern holy grass, a rare grass, growing by the Thurso river. He taught himself botany and geology by walking up to fifty miles in a day.
He sent his fossils to Hugh Miller, the great geologist, and Miller wrote about him. Dick never wanted fame. He just wanted to know what was under the next stone. A good way to live.
